title: Renewal Processes and Long-Run Reward
engineName: Track repeated renewals using inter-arrival times, renewal counts and long-run averages.
objectives: Define a renewal process from iid positive inter-renewal times.
Construct renewal epochs and the counting process N(t).
Distinguish inter-arrival time, renewal count and renewal function.
Use the renewal equation and elementary renewal theorem in elementary cases.

prereq.name: IID random variables
prereq.why: Successive gaps are iid in the ordinary renewal model.

prereq.name: Expectation and distribution functions
prereq.why: Renewal counts and long-run rates use expectations and distribution functions.

prereq.name: Poisson process
prereq.why: A Poisson process is a special renewal process with exponential gaps.

traps: Renewal epochs are cumulative sums, not individual gaps.
N(t) counts renewals by t; m(t)=E[N(t)] is the renewal function.
The long-run renewal rate is 1/μ, not μ.
The elementary renewal theorem is asymptotic, not an exact finite-time formula.
howto: Define iid positive gaps Xᵢ; form Sₙ=ΣXᵢ; count N(t)=max{n:Sₙ≤t}; calculate μ=E[X]; use 1/μ for long-run renewal rate and E[R]/μ for long-run reward.

sheet: X₁,X₂,… are iid positive inter-renewal times with mean μ=E[X₁].
Exponential iid gaps give a Poisson process.
tricks: Draw the timeline before counting N(t).
Include an event exactly at t because Sₙ≤t.
Invert the mean gap for the long-run rate.
Do not use the Poisson count formula for a general renewal process.
shortcuts: Exponential gaps of rate λ: E[N(t)]=λt.
remember: IID gaps are central to the ordinary renewal model.
Long-run results do not determine all finite-time probabilities.
The finite-time renewal count depends on the full inter-renewal distribution.

scenes.title: Refresh cumulative waiting times
body: Successive cycle lengths are X₁,X₂,… . The time of the second event is S₂=X₁+X₂; the time of the nth event is Sₙ=X₁+⋯+Xₙ.
A gap is a duration. An epoch is the cumulative time at which an event occurs.

items.ask: If gaps are 3 and 5 hours, when does renewal 2 occur?
refresh: Start from the meaning of a duration between events. For example, if a component works for 3 hours after one replacement and then for 5 hours after the next, the two cycle lengths are X₁=3 and X₂=5. The first renewal epoch is S₁=3, while the second is S₂=3+5=8 hours. This distinction between a gap and a cumulative event time is used throughout the lesson.

items.ask: If X₁=2, X₂=4 and X₃=1, find S₃.
refresh: A cumulative sum adds every completed inter-renewal time up to the event being considered. If X₁=2, X₂=4 and X₃=1, then S₁=2, S₂=2+4=6 and S₃=2+4+1=7. The third renewal does not occur after only the third gap; it occurs after all three gaps have elapsed.

items.ask: If X is 1 or 3 with equal probability, find E[X].
refresh: For a discrete random variable, expectation is the probability-weighted average. If X is 1 with probability one-half and 3 with probability one-half, then E[X]=1(1/2)+3(1/2)=2. This mean gap is denoted μ and later its reciprocal gives the long-run renewal rate.

ask.q: What is the difference between an inter-renewal time and a renewal epoch?
ask.nudge: One is a single duration; the other is the cumulative time from the start.

scenes.title: A system that renews repeatedly
body: A renewal may represent replacing a failed component, completing a repair or replenishing stock. Each renewal begins a fresh cycle.
The ordinary model assumes cycle lengths are iid positive random variables. If the distribution changes from cycle to cycle, the ordinary model may not apply.

scenario.title: Count completed service cycles
body: A reliability team monitors a fleet of identical pumps. Whenever a pump fails, it is repaired or replaced and a new operating cycle begins. The operating duration from the end of one repair to the next failure is recorded as a cycle length.

Let X₁,X₂,… denote successive cycle lengths. The first replacement occurs at S₁=X₁, the second at S₂=X₁+X₂, and the nth at Sₙ=X₁+⋯+Xₙ. A time horizon t may contain a random number of completed replacements.

The ordinary renewal model treats these cycle lengths as independent and identically distributed positive random variables. This is an idealisation: if the pump ages and its failure distribution changes after each repair, the iid assumption may fail and a different reliability model may be needed.

The model is useful when a renewal restores the system to a statistically comparable starting condition. It separates the duration of one cycle from the count of cycles completed over a long operating period.
scenario.q: What does one renewal cycle measure?
scenario.answer: The time from one renewal to the next.

ask.q: What is the mathematical assumption about successive cycle lengths?
ask.nudge: The ordinary model uses a common distribution and independence.

scenes.title: Formal definition of a renewal process
body: Let X₁,X₂,… be iid positive inter-renewal times with distribution F and finite mean μ=E[X₁] when finite-mean results are used.
Renewal epochs: S₀=0 and Sₙ=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ. Counting process: N(t)=max{n:Sₙ≤t}. Renewal function: m(t)=E[N(t)].

blocks.body: X₁,X₂,… are iid positive random variables with distribution F. Their common mean is μ=E[X₁], when finite.
S₀=0 and Sₙ=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ for n≥1. Each epoch is measured from the initial time origin.
N(t)=max{n≥0:Sₙ≤t}. It counts completed renewals, including an event exactly at t.
m(t)=E[N(t)] is the expected number of renewals by time t. N(t) is random; m(t) is deterministic for a specified model.

ask.q: Why is m(t) not the same thing as N(t)?
ask.nudge: Compare a random realised count with its expected value.

scenes.title: Worked example: deterministic gaps
body: If every inter-renewal time is c=4 hours, then S₁=4, S₂=8 and S₃=12.
At t=11, exactly two epochs have occurred, so N(11)=2. The definition includes events exactly at t.
scenes.problem: A component is replaced exactly every 4 hours. Find S₁,S₂,S₃ and N(11).

ask.q: What is N(12) if replacements occur exactly at 4, 8 and 12 hours?
ask.nudge: The definition counts epochs satisfying Sₙ≤t.

scenes.title: Renewal counts and their distribution
body: N(t)≥n if and only if Sₙ≤t. Exactly n renewals means Sₙ≤t<Sₙ₊₁.
For random gaps, the cumulative epochs and therefore the number of renewals by a fixed t are random.

blocks.body: N(t)≥n if and only if Sₙ≤t. The nth renewal must have occurred by time t.
N(t)=n if and only if Sₙ≤t<Sₙ₊₁. The nth event has occurred but the next has not.
If the inter-renewal times are random, the cumulative epochs are random. Consequently N(t), the number of epochs before the fixed horizon, is a random variable.

ask.q: Express N(t)=n using Sₙ and Sₙ₊₁.
ask.nudge: The nth event has happened, but event n+1 has not.

scenes.title: Worked example: exponential gaps
body: If iid gaps are exponential with rate λ, the renewal counting process is a homogeneous Poisson process.
For λ=3 per hour and t=2 hours, E[N(2)]=λt=6. This formula is specific to exponential gaps.
scenes.problem: Inter-renewal times are iid exponential with rate 3 per hour. Find E[N(2)].

steps.say: Exponential iid gaps define a Poisson process.
steps.why: This is the special renewal model.
The expected count equals rate times duration.

ask.q: Does every renewal process have Poisson counts?
ask.nudge: What special distribution must the iid gaps have for the Poisson case?

scenario.teaser: A help desk receives calls with exponential gaps
scenario.title: A Poisson arrival stream as a renewal model
body: A help desk receives incoming calls. Suppose the time between consecutive calls is independent and exponentially distributed with rate λ calls per hour. Each new call starts the next inter-arrival interval.

Exponential iid inter-arrival times define a homogeneous Poisson process. Therefore the number of calls in an interval of length t has a Poisson distribution with mean λt, and its expected count is λt.
For example, at λ=3 calls per hour, the expected number in a two-hour interval is six. This does not mean exactly six calls will arrive; it is the expectation over repeated intervals under the model.
This is a special case of renewal theory. A general renewal process may have non-exponential iid gaps and will not, in general, have Poisson counts.
scenario.close: The exponential-gap model links renewal theory to the Poisson process.

scenes.title: The renewal equation
body: Let F(t)=P(X₁≤t). The renewal function satisfies m(t)=F(t)+∫₀ᵗm(t−x)dF(x).
Condition on the first gap x: if the first renewal occurs at x, the remaining time is t−x and the expected subsequent count is m(t−x).

blocks.body: Let F(t)=P(X₁≤t) be the distribution function of one cycle length.
m(t)=F(t)+∫₀ᵗm(t−x)dF(x). The first term accounts for a first renewal by t; the integral accounts for subsequent renewals after the first gap.
If the first cycle lasts x, then t−x time remains after that renewal. The expected number of further renewals is m(t−x). Averaging over the first-gap distribution gives the integral.

ask.q: What does the term F(t) represent in the renewal equation?
ask.nudge: It is the probability that the first cycle has finished by time t.

scenes.title: Fixed gaps versus random gaps
body: A deterministic gap gives regular epochs and N(t)=⌊t/c⌋. Random gaps create variable spacing.
Two models can have the same mean gap but different finite-time count distributions. The mean alone does not determine every finite-time probability.

blocks.body: If every gap equals c, then the epochs occur at c, 2c, 3c,… and N(t)=⌊t/c⌋.
For random cycle lengths, the distribution of N(t) depends on the full distribution of the cumulative sums Sₙ.

blocks.h: Same mean does not mean same finite-time law
blocks.body: Two renewal models can have the same mean gap and the same long-run renewal rate, yet different finite-time count distributions.

ask.q: Does knowing only E[X] determine P(N(5)=2) for every renewal model?
ask.nudge: Finite-time probabilities depend on more than the mean.

scenario.teaser: Two replacement policies have different variability
scenario.title: Same average life, different short-term behaviour
body: Consider two component-replacement policies with the same average cycle duration. One policy produces nearly regular lifetimes; the other has much more variable lifetimes. Both can have the same long-run renewal rate under the elementary renewal theorem.

At a short fixed horizon, however, the number of replacements can differ because the distributions of the cumulative epochs are different. Knowing only the mean cycle length does not determine the full distribution of N(t).

This distinction matters when a maintenance planner needs a finite-horizon probability, such as the chance of at least two failures before a scheduled inspection. The complete inter-renewal distribution is then needed, not just its mean.
The long-run theorem is valuable for average planning over long periods, while finite-time risk questions require distribution-specific analysis.
scenario.close: The mean controls the asymptotic rate, not every finite-time probability.

scenes.title: Elementary renewal theorem
body: Under standard conditions for iid positive gaps with finite mean μ, the elementary renewal theorem states m(t)/t→1/μ as t→∞.
The long-run renewal rate is the reciprocal of the mean cycle length. This is an asymptotic result, not an exact finite-time formula.

ask.q: If the mean gap is 2.5 days, what is the long-run rate per day?

flow.caption: From the cycle-length distribution to a long-run rate

nodes.label: If reward R per cycle: E[R]/μ

blocks.body: For iid positive inter-renewal times with finite mean μ, under standard conditions, m(t)/t tends to 1/μ as t tends to infinity.
The expected number of renewals per unit time approaches the reciprocal of the mean cycle length. The units are renewals per unit time.
The theorem describes a limiting average. It does not assert that m(t)=t/μ for every finite t or that N(t) is non-random.

scenes.title: Guided problem: long-run rate
body: Let X be 1 hour with probability 1/4 and 3 hours with probability 3/4. Then μ=1/4+9/4=5/2 hours.
The long-run rate is 1/μ=2/5 renewals per hour. The mean gap is a time; its reciprocal is a rate.
scenes.problem: X is 1 hour with probability 1/4 and 3 hours with probability 3/4. Find the long-run renewal rate.

solution.say: The elementary renewal theorem gives rate 1/μ.
The rate is 2/5 renewals per hour.

ask.q: Why do we invert the mean gap to obtain a rate?
ask.nudge: A rate counts cycles per unit time, while μ measures time per cycle.

scenes.title: Renewal-reward theorem
body: If R is the reward earned in one cycle and X is its length, the renewal-reward theorem gives long-run reward per unit time E[R]/E[X], under standard iid-cycle and integrability conditions.
Use expected reward per cycle divided by expected cycle duration.

blocks.body: Let Rᵢ be the reward earned during cycle i, paired with cycle length Xᵢ. Assume iid cycles and the standard finite-expectation conditions.
Long-run reward per unit time = E[R]/E[X].
Divide the average reward earned per cycle by the average time consumed per cycle. This is a long-run average rate.

ask.q: If expected reward is 12 and mean cycle duration is 3 hours, find the long-run reward rate.

scenes.title: Guided problem: reward rate
body: A system earns expected reward 100 units per cycle and has expected cycle duration 5 hours.
The long-run reward rate is 100/5=20 units per hour.
scenes.problem: Expected reward per cycle is 100 units and expected cycle duration is 5 hours. Find the long-run reward rate.

solution.say: Divide expected reward per cycle by expected cycle duration.

ask.q: If expected cycle duration doubles while expected reward stays fixed, what happens to the long-run reward rate?

scenes.title: Exam traps and interpretation checks
body: Renewal epochs are cumulative sums, N(t) is a count, and m(t)=E[N(t)] is an expected count.
The long-run rate is 1/μ, not μ. A Poisson process is a special renewal process, not the only renewal process.
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false.

items.why: Sₙ is the sum of the first n gaps.

items.claim: N(t) counts renewals completed by t.
items.why: It counts epochs not exceeding t.
Only exponential iid gaps give the Poisson process.

scenes.title: Summary and supplementary status
scenes.objective: Recall the key results and scope.
body: Start with iid positive gaps; form Sₙ; count N(t); and distinguish the random count from m(t)=E[N(t)].

The elementary renewal theorem gives rate 1/E[X]. The renewal-reward theorem gives E[R]/E[X]. This lesson is supplementary: renewal processes are not explicitly named in the official Unit IX syllabus shared for this project.
